segments.text: Trefgann

"The armored man came down the hill, He came to take, he came to kill. He knocked upon the Iron Gate, We told him he would have to wait. He huffed and puffed and broke his bone, and now we use his head for stone! One step! Two step! Three steps! Four! Don't come knocking at our door!"
Playground skipping-song heard in Llyra
Concord of War
Remosa's open wound. They can't stop scratching it, and Trefgann has been opened and bled again and again and again. No wonder they can't think of themselves as anything but "not Remosa".

Hillside forests the color of green rust, lakes rippling in the spring breeze, soil which smells of musty thyme, laced with an ancient road paved in marble. The Trefganners cling to a sense of simplicity, directness, freedom, maybe?

Hardy people, weaponized working folk, sitting inside one of Virelia's greatest regions and too busy surveying Remosa to realize it. Too busy taking apart and mocking the ancient statues to marvel at their beauty.

Maybe fittingly, the opposite of Remosa's hubris has taken the form of paranoia. I realize I'm painting a bleak picture here. And perhaps, an unfair one. The Trefganners are decent folk. Tight communities, strong agricultural identity, great tobacco.
There's just something to be said about people who'd scorn anything and everything as long as it has a Remosan accent.
Tobacco and Stew

Since it seems everyone in Trefgann agrees on politics, what's left to argue about is mostly food, followed by tobacco. Strangers, lucky for them, are unburdened with this until it is proven they have nothing to do with Remosa.

You'll get stared at for three days, and if you pass they'll give you the nods, then the endless inescapable war stories. If you don't, the staring never stops. As a side note, the food is surprisingly pretty good.
A typical Trefganni meal consists of steamed root vegetables and lake fish, hard bread on the side, swallowed with the help of cool buckwheat beer. Lovely, if you can ignore the stares.

Trefganners are the only nation I've seen where people are so damn proud of their land. They learn it by heart, each tree and every abandoned piece of infrastructure. A habit born of farming and foraging, which ended up winning the war for them.

Despite that, the Trefganners show an utter lack of care for what the empire left behind and three wars then added to the pile. It's all still out there, unstable, deteriorating, and when used correctly, hazardous to the uninitiated.
More Remosan soldiers have died in the sewers beneath Brenmath than in its fields.
A Crown of Mud
Brenmath was the seat of the empire for most of recorded history. The court governed from there, and the wealth of half a continent flowed through the gates the Trefganners would eventually shut.

Then came the Witch-Wars, and the boneheaded, bizarre edict to expand the empire onto Myrskov. The records of that particular council meeting make one wonder if there is still hope for our species. Fucking morons.

Trefganner conscripts died in those forests for a campaign the empire had no chance of winning, fed by crops their families needed at home. The Witch Wars had already been draining the province for generations before that.

The costs always fell downward, while the taxes, as always, trickled up. Yet the guild-masters and mayors still somehow persevered, and kept things below boiling point. Until Remosa finally admitted it really had no business in Myrskov, and the outrage struck.
Imperial administrators were dragged from their offices. Noble families who had governed from Brenmath for generations were slaughtered in the streets.

Property was seized, estates burned, and anyone with the wrong name or the wrong accent learned quickly which way the path to Tharlin's Crossing ran. Guild-masters, mayors, trade leaders, all met in "purified" Brenmath and formally declared the empire to be no more.
Varenhal, the empire's own civic Graith, read his mantras and concluded the empire had made itself incompatible with them. The gates closed shut. That is one door that will never open again.

Three times since, the empire has marched east to take the capital back. Each time smaller, more desperate. Each time eating mud from the soil the Trefganners knew better than the people who ruled it. The third was fifty years ago.
The fourth is expected within the lifetime of the current generation. Whether it will come is a question for Ezgarin. Whether Trefgann will be ready is not a question at all.
Pecking Order

Much like the farmers market that is Southfield's ruling council, the Synod of Secession is comprised mostly of people who have no business holding a pen. They convene when the situation demands and are otherwise content to let things sort themselves out.

Four cities, four delegates each, comfortably, or perhaps better described, uncomfortably, sit in a senate hall built for three hundred imperial administrators. They settle trade disputes, and occasionally make a failed attempt at something that requires coordination across city lines.
In brief, the Blackhens handle executive defense. Everything else is either local, mismanaged, or both.

Past the cities, governance thins out fast. Towns and villages answer to whichever city claims them, or to no-one if the claim was never pressed. The militia is the one thing that reaches everywhere: everyone can wield a weapon, and are quick to draw it.
And when the call goes out, the region can pull itself together in days.

One point that I unfortunately can't skim over is Blank. A stable rift that strips identity. Cross its boundary and you are still a person, in some sense of the word. You simply have no idea which one. The Trefganni cities use it to dispose of criminals they deem unsalvageable.
Critics often say it's no different than execution. Less filth, but no less vulgar. I, for one, think they can at least be commended for their CREATIVITY.
Think of The Children

The Third March was fifty years ago, long enough for the current crop of Trefganni youth to have fathers who mostly remember having spears shoved into their arms whenever it rained too hard. Habits hold better than memories, and Trefgann is a land of habit, after all.

Offensive spells are still considered inappropriate while few remember the trauma that fueled the taboo. Children learn the Marches before they understand them, and are constantly warned of what's to come.
The result is not obedience, to no one's surprise but the Trefganni. Young ones rebel, old ones complain, as is the natural order of things.

The rebellion takes many forms: eye-rolls during drills, Remosan literature, the quiet departure of young spellcasters who wish to learn "real" magic, and also the occasional argument that the gate should, in fact, open both ways. You know how it is. This is not policy, thank fuck.

It is mostly tavern courage, fueled by ale, boredom and youth. The elders call them westward fools. Some have started using the name proudly, proving that Trefgann has preserved its children from Remosa but not from stupidity.
In summary, peace had raised a generation that knows war through stories only, which is to say they know it very well and not at all.
Rumors

The Iron Giant: A war-construct from the First March has turned up in old Fionn's field outside Elidyr. Dormant, but the core is still hot. He wants to strip it for parts, But Oifara, the local village head, fears it might trigger something that levels the town.

The Peddler's Tin: A Haldrithian peddler sold tin boxes to three villages along the Quiet Road. Keeps grain fresh, he said. Worked, too. Then the wheat in Rhiannon's storehouse sprouted overnight and cracked the walls open, and the peddler is nowhere to be found.

The Beacons: Someone's been carving imperial survey markers into the milestones along the Quiet Road. A unit on patrol spotted the first one three weeks ago and took a chisel to it. Next morning it was back, cut deeper than before.

The Hidden Cache: A village bell rang last month. A kid's prank, false alarm. However, as result it turned out that Vanguard has enough weaponry to arm a small army. Much more than a village its size should. The Synod wants answers.

The Runaway: An eleven-year-old boy named Erik has escaped Cadfael village with nothing but the clothes on his back. His family is rightfully worried, but the other children of the village say it's better that way since he was "a witch".
